 Home / News & Rumors / Disgruntled Ex-Disney CEO Bob Chapek’s Book Bombs Disgruntled Ex-Disney CEO Bob Chapek’s Book Bombs
 By Tom Bricker 
 October 13, 2026 October 13, 2026 
 34 Comments 
 Former Disney CEO Bob Chapek has denied himself of his  happily ever after . The ex-executive’s tell-all memoir covering his rise, fall, and supposed scapegoating has bombed, with more people watching one of the long-forgotten, circa-2021 Disney+ shows that he greenlit than have read his book.
 This is the latest development in the Disney’s Bob Swap™️ drama, which has been rebooted and adapted for bookshelves. With the publishing of Chapek’s book, the Days of Our Disney Lives soap opera has been renewed for another season, and Christmas has come early to the lovers of chaos and cattiness out there. I know this is about as tortured as Chapek’s writing, but his reemergence really has been the gift that keeps on giving.
 It started a couple weeks ago with Bob Chapek’s media blitz. His media appearances and interviews were an unmitigated disaster, to put it mildly. Chapek wrote this book to tell his side of the story in order to rehabilitate his image, reframe his legacy at Disney, and make himself hireable again. He accomplished exactly zero of that with his first public appearances in nearly 4 years.
 If anything, Chapek came across considerably worse than he did in 2022. It’s as if what we saw when he was Disney CEO was the most media trained and personable the Bobot2000 could be. During the last few years of seclusion, he’s reverted back to his factory defaults.
 I can’t help but wonder if he even has advisors or a communications team at this point, because it sure doesn’t seem like it. He has made perplexing decision after perplexing decision, with my favorite still being his interview with something called “Valuetainment for Gen-Z.” (Seriously, it’s worth a watch.)
 Another high note was the most Chapek quote of all-time in an interview with Bloomberg : “I love private equity.” An appearance on CNBC was awkward and defensive, and the throughline of all of these interviews has been zero accountability for what went wrong and a vendetta against Bob Iger, who lives rent-free in his head. (Understandably so, in fairness.)
 Chapek has defended the wrong decisions, doubled-down on his penchant for price increases and cost-cutting, and continued to express his open disdain for Disney fans. Everything he has said thus far reinforces his own past admissions that he has low EQ or emotional intelligence, and is oddly proud of it.
 If anything, the biggest takeaway has been an indictment of Bob Iger’s judgment. How could he talk to Chapek for more than 10 minutes and come away thinking Chapek would be suitable as the public face of the Walt Disney Company?! Beyond a shadow of a doubt, Bob Chapek has proven that he did not and still does not “get” what made Disney… Disney . 
 While I’m not so surprised by just how painful Chapek’s media tour was to watch and read, I honestly am somewhat surprised by how badly his book has sold. If anything, the trainwreck made me more excited for his memoir, as it was abundantly clear Chapek wasn’t publishing a puff piece. He was going scorched earth, and it was going to be a mess! As it turns out, not all publicity is good publicity .
 The latest development comes via Hollywood insider Matthew Belloni of Puck News , who among other things knew about Disneyland Abu Dhabi before its announcement and that Josh D’Amaro would be named Disney CEO (with Dana Walden sticking around) before that happened. He’s also been covering Bob Iger’s fight to bury Robbie Whelan’s upcoming book: The House of Mouse: Bob Iger and The War of Succession at Disney .
 Belloni reports that, Bob Chapek’s memoir, Behind the Castle Walls: My Thirty Years at the Happiest Place on Earth , only sold approximately 2,400 copies during its first week of sales. Ouch . Belloni attributes this stat to BookScan, which is the publishing industry’s go-to data service that tracks weekly point-of-sale retail purchases.
 This would seem to be accurate. Chapek’s book failed to make the top 10 on the  New York Times nonfiction best sellers list. It’s unclear where, if at all, it did rank on the list during its first week, but it currently isn’t there at all.
 If you’re looking for a more positive spin,  Behind the Castle Walls  is currently #1 on Amazon. Well, its list of Business Ethics books. For whatever it’s worth, #2 is a book from 2008 and #4 is about the fall of Enron. I guess that just proves if you narrow the parameters enough, anything can be the best!
 Meanwhile, Chapek’s book is #6 in Biographies of Business & Industrial Professionals and #437 in Humor & Entertainment. (There are parts of it that made me laugh out loud!). On Amazon’s overall best sellers list, Behind the Castle Walls ranks #4,038. Double ouch!
 At risk of stating the obvious, all of these numbers are really bad. I am shocked that it only sold 2,400 copies, and can’t help but wonder what percentage of those were bought be people who work for Disney or in the Hollywood and/or blogging trades. I would’ve bet that 10,000 copies would’ve been sold in Burbank alone!
 It’s less surprising that Disney fans didn’t buy what Bob was selling. Far and away the top response we heard when “recommending” the book has been that fans were not going to give that man another dollar. Some said they’d check it out from the library, but most refused to purchase on principle. Even more indicated, flatly, that they had no desire to read Chapek’s side of the story.
 If you’re inclined to take pity on Bob Chapek or view this pile-on as a bit mean-spirited, need we remind you of just how much pain he inflicted on Disney fans during his reign of terror? Or how he has zero remorse for it, and feels like he did nothing wrong?! (Seriously, two of the themes of his book is that “I was right all along” and “it was someone else’s fault.”)
 If that doesn’t do the trick, just keep in mind that Bob Chapek was paid $20 million in severance to go away and received north of $100 million in compensation during his time in the c-suite. He didn’t write this book for the money in the first place; he did it for image rehabilitation. As it turns out, he’ll get neither.
 Chapek’s memoir is published by Gallery Books, a major publishing imprint of Simon & Schuster. It’s co-written by Don Yaeger, a New York Times bestselling author and longtime associate editor at Sports Illustrated .   It appears that co-writing books with media figures is kind of Yaeger’s thing .
 Behind the Castle Walls  currently has a 4.0 review score on Amazon from 65 reviews and a 3.2 on Goodreads. In combing through those out of curiosity, it does not appear to be a ‘review bombing’ situation. People just don’t like the book.
 To put that into perspective, Bob Iger’s  Ride of a Lifetime   has a 4.8 rating on Amazon from over 24,000 reviews and a 4.4 on Goodreads.  DisneyWar   sits at 4.6 on Amazon and 4.1 on Goodreads despite being far and away the best book of the trio. Meanwhile, Joe Rohde’s new book,  Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagineering the Impossible , holds an impressive 4.8 and 4.6 score.
 I’m only partially through Behind the Castle Walls  (it’s been a busy few weeks), and probably won’t get around to doing a full review of it. After all, so many of you have already said there’s no way you’ll buy it, so what’s the point? Instead, I’ll share a quick capsule review here.
 Thus far, I’m really enjoying  Behind the Castle Walls. Seriously! It is shocking candid, contains countless interesting anecdotes, and gives insight into Chapek’s thinking. It’s a really fascinating read, and clearly was not polished by a PR team or editors trying to massage the messaging. The book is unpolished and rough around the edges (mostly in a good way); it’s easy to read and is a page turner.
 Whereas Iger’s memoir is more calculated and offers leadership lessons, this feels less contrived, for lack of a better word. There have already been a few occasions when I’ve wondered “why would you publish these words?!” It feels like a quasi DisneyWar spin-off or sequel, but written by one of the main characters who didn’t quite comprehend how to paint himself as a sympathetic figure. This is good for readers, as we’re getting something closer to being unvarnished.
 With that said, I would only recommend this book to those who remember living through the Chapek era and have a decent degree of media literacy. The most charitable framing is that Chapek is an unreliable narrator of his own story. He’s like the Holden Caulfield of former CEOs. The less charitable take is that he’s telling half truths or lying by omission.
 I can’t speak to his state of mind, so it’s unclear which is actually the case, but I’m inclined to believe Chapek is “only” an unreliable narrator. There’s too much truth-telling that amounts to statements against his own self interest. Regardless, it’s critical to understand this so you don’t take what he’s saying at face value, as at least some of his claims are false or misleading.
 This is simply Chapek’s recollection of what transpired; the contemporaneous record calls a lot of it into question. I suspect the independent House of Mouse: Bob Iger and The War of Succession at Disney book will offer even better balance and fact-checking.
 The most interesting tidbits thus far have come from earlier in Chapek’s career when he helmed the home entertainment and video division, perfected the “Disney Vault” strategy, and began his corporate ascent.
 From this and other comments he made during his time at Parks & Resorts, it’s very clear that Chapek was an astute businessman. When playing to his strengths, he was incredibly successful and there can be little doubt about his acumen. The problems came when he was elevated to public-facing positions and his worst impulses went unchecked.
 Towards the end of his tenure as CEO, it became increasingly clear that Chapek had lost the plot. He became outwardly defensive, openly faulting fans for not comprehending his approach. I was never a fan of Chapek, but I’ve previously pointed to this October 2022 WSJ conference as the point where he completely and irrevocably lost me. Chapek’s book is basically a continuation of that. It’s unfortunate that he hasn’t taken the time for self-reflection or introspection in the years since.
 Ultimately, I am looking forward to finishing Behind the Castle Walls: My Thirty Years at the Happiest Place on Earth .  I’m a sucker for the palace intrigue that unfolded behind the scenes during this tumultuous time. It was rough to live through, and I still have an intense dislike for Bob Chapek, and his complete lack of self-awareness or reflection. It seems that, 4 years later, he hasn’t changed much.
 However, enough time has passed that it’s cathartic to hear Chapek’s side of the story, and see the extent to which that’s divorced from reality. It’s also fascinating to see how he views decisions that are clearly negative from my perspective as things about which he should boast.
 There are anecdotes that are interesting, but the best part of the book thus far has been the window into the fantasyland of Chapek’s mind. I’m not sure how many fans want to look through that, though, which probably explains the low sales stats. To each their own, but I think it’s a delightful trainwreck. This is my version of guilty-pleasure reality television hate-watching.
